subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 48-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C virus infection presents with blistering lesions on the dorsum of his hands following sun exposure. He notes that minor trauma causes superficial skin erosions that heal with scarring, hyperpigmentation, and tiny white papules (milia). He also reports that his urine appears dark reddish-brown ('tea-colored'). Physical examination reveals tense vesicles, crusts, and hypertrichosis on his malar cheeks. Serum ferritin is 680 ng/mL (elevated). Wood lamp examination of the urine demonstrates bright coral-pink fluorescence. Which of the following enzymes is deficient in this patient's hepatocytes?

options.text: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) in the cytosolic heme synthesis pathway
options.explanation: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria, caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD). UROD catalyzes the sequential decarboxylation of four acetate side chains of uroporphyrinogen III to methyl groups, forming coproporphyrinogen III. Hepatic iron overload, alcohol, and hepatitis C trigger generation of reactive oxygen species that inhibit UROD. Uroporphyrinogen accumulates, oxidizes to uroporphyrin, and circulates to the skin. Exposure to long-wave UV light (Soret band ~400 nm) excites uroporphyrin, producing reactive oxygen species, blister formation, skin fragility, and coral-pink fluorescent tea-colored urine.

options.text: Porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase) in the cytoplasm
options.explanation: PBGD deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), which presents with acute neurovisceral attacks (abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychosis) WITHOUT cutaneous photosensitivity or skin blisters.

options.text: Delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) in the cytoplasm
options.explanation: ALAD deficiency is extremely rare and inhibited by lead; it causes neurovisceral symptoms without prominent blistering PCT photosensitivity.

options.text: Ferrochelatase in the inner mitochondrial membrane
options.explanation: Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), which presents with painful burning/erythema immediately upon sun exposure, without tense blisters or chronic tea-colored urine.

options.text: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase in the mitochondrial membrane
options.explanation: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency causes variegate porphyria, which combines neurovisceral attacks with cutaneous photosensitivity, unlike pure cutaneous PCT.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of severe, colicky, diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Over the past 2 days, she has become increasingly agitated, anxious, and paranoid. She began a strict low-carbohydrate, fasting weight-loss diet 5 days ago and was prescribed rifampin for meningococcal exposure 2 days ago. Physical examination shows tachycardia (pulse 118/min) and mild bilateral wrist drop; abdominal examination reveals no tenderness, guarding, or peritoneal signs despite severe subjective agony. Urinalysis appears normal initially, but after standing in sunlight for 2 hours, the urine turns dark port-wine colored. Cutaneous examination shows completely normal skin without blisters or photosensitivity. Which of the following is the underlying enzymatic defect in this patient?

options.text: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) in hepatocytes
options.explanation: UROD deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda with prominent blistering cutaneous photosensitivity, unlike AIP which has purely neurovisceral symptoms.

options.text: Porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD / hydroxymethylbilane synthase) in the heme biosynthetic pathway
options.explanation: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by haploinsufficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD). Fasting and CYP450-inducing drugs (rifampin, antiepileptics, barbiturates) deplete hepatic free heme, disinhibiting the rate-limiting enzyme ALAS1. This causes massive upstream accumulation of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). ALA and PBG are direct neurotoxins causing the 5 P's: Painful abdomen (out of proportion to exam), Polyneuropathy (wrist/foot drop), Psychosis/agitation, Port-wine colored urine (PBG oxidizes to porphobilin on light exposure), and Precipitation by drugs/fasting. Crucially, because the block is prior to porphyrin ring formation, THERE IS NO CUTANEOUS PHOTOSENSITIVITY. Treatment includes IV glucose (inhibits ALAS1 via PGC-1alpha downregulation) and IV hemin.

options.text: Delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase 1 (ALAS1) in the mitochondria
options.explanation: ALAS1 is the rate-limiting enzyme that is HYPERACTIVATED (disinhibited) during an acute attack; it is not the deficient enzyme.

options.text: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase in the mitochondrial intermembrane space
options.explanation: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency causes hereditary coproporphyria, which features both neurovisceral crises and cutaneous photosensitivity.

options.text: Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase in the tyrosine degradation pathway
options.explanation: Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency causes alkaptonuria, characterized by urine turning black on standing, ochronosis, and arthropathy, without acute neurovisceral agony.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Phenylketonuria PAH vs BH4 Cofactor Deficiency
stem: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the clinic for developmental delay. He was born at home in another country and did not undergo newborn screening. Physical examination shows fair skin, blonde hair, blue eyes, and eczema, despite both parents having dark hair and brown eyes. The infant has profound cognitive impairment, hyperreflexia, and a distinct 'mousy' or 'musty' body odor. Serum amino acid analysis demonstrates a phenylalanine concentration of 1,200 micromol/L (normal < 120 micromol/L) and a tyrosine concentration of 25 micromol/L (depressed; normal 40-100 micromol/L). Oral administration of sapropterin (tetrahydrobiopterin, BH4) for 48 hours fails to lower serum phenylalanine concentrations. Which of the following is the primary defective enzyme in this infant, and what dietary amino acid alteration is mandatory?

options.text: Deficiency of dihydropteridine reductase; tyrosine must be restricted while phenylalanine is supplemented
options.explanation: Dihydropteridine reductase deficiency impairs BH4 recycling and responds to BH4/neurotransmitter precursors; moreover, tyrosine must be supplemented, not restricted.

options.text: Deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase; phenylalanine and tyrosine must both be completely eliminated from the diet
options.explanation: Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency causes alkaptonuria with ochronosis, not infantile cognitive impairment and musty odor.

options.text: Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (classical PKU); tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid that must be supplemented, while dietary phenylalanine is strictly restricted
options.explanation: Classical phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine in the liver. When PAH is nonfunctional, phenylalanine accumulates and is shunted into phenylketones (phenylacetate, phenyllactate, phenylpyruvate), producing profound neurotoxicity, seizures, microcephaly, and a musty body odor. Excess phenylalanine competitively inhibits tyrosinase, impairing melanin synthesis (fair skin, blonde hair). Because tyrosine cannot be synthesized from phenylalanine, TYROSINE BECOMES AN ESSENTIAL AMINO ACID and must be supplemented, while phenylalanine intake must be strictly restricted. Lack of response to BH4 excludes dihydropteridine reductase or BH4 synthesis defects.

options.text: Deficiency of branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase; leucine, isoleucine, and valine must be strictly restricted
options.explanation: BCKDH deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease with sweet-smelling urine and ketoacidosis, not classic PKU.

options.text: Deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase; succinylacetone must be administered as an essential metabolite
options.explanation: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes tyrosinemia type 1 with hepatic failure and renal Fanconi syndrome; succinylacetone is a toxic metabolite, not a treatment.

explanation: Classical phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine in the liver. When PAH is nonfunctional, phenylalanine accumulates and is shunted into phenylketones (phenylacetate, phenyllactate, phenylpyruvate), producing profound neurotoxicity, seizures, microcephaly, and a musty body odor. Excess phenylalanine competitively inhibits tyrosinase, impairing melanin synthesis (fair skin, blonde hair). Because tyrosine cannot be synthesized from phenylalanine, TYROSINE BECOMES AN ESSENTIAL AMINO ACID and must be supplemented, while phenylalanine intake must be strictly restricted. Lack of response to BH4 excludes dihydropteridine reductase or BH4 synthesis defects. Musty odor + fair skin/blonde hair + severe developmental delay + high phenylalanine/low tyrosine + no response to BH4 = Classical PKU -> PAH deficiency, tyrosine is essential.
objective: Understand and correctly identify the clinical, diagnostic, and pathophysiological principles of Phenylketonuria PAH vs BH4 Cofactor Deficiency.
keyPoints: Phenylketonuria PAH vs BH4 Cofactor Deficiency
Musty odor + fair skin/blonde hair + severe developmental delay + high phenylalanine/low tyrosine + no response to BH4 = Classical PKU -> PAH deficiency, tyrosine is essential.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Maple Syrup Urine Disease BCKDH Complex Defect
stem: A 5-day-old male infant born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy becomes increasingly lethargic and feeds poorly. On physical examination, he is stuporous with alternating episodes of hypertonia and hypotonia ('dystonia'), and his diapers emit a distinct sweet odor resembling burnt sugar or maple syrup. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: blood glucose 58 mg/dL, arterial blood gas showing pH 7.22, PaCO2 24 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 10 mEq/L (anion gap metabolic acidosis), and ketonuria. Serum amino acid chromatography reveals massive elevations in leucine, isoleucine, and valine, as well as the presence of alloisoleucine. Which of the following vitamin-derived cofactors is an obligatory component of the multienzyme complex defective in this infant?

options.text: Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP, derived from vitamin B6)
options.explanation: PLP is the cofactor for transaminases (e.g. branched-chain amino acid transaminase), which convert BCAAs to alpha-keto acids upstream of the defective BCKDH complex.

options.text: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)
options.explanation: BH4 is the cofactor for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan), not branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenases.

options.text: Adenosylcobalamin (derived from vitamin B12)
options.explanation: Adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, defective in methylmalonic acidemia, not MSUD.

options.text: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, derived from vitamin B1)
options.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) complex. BCKDH metabolizes the alpha-keto acids derived from BRANCHED-CHAIN AMINO ACIDS: Leucine (alpha-ketoisocaproate), Isoleucine (alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate), and Valine (alpha-ketoisovalerate). Like pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (alpha-KGDH), the BCKDH complex requires five obligatory cofactors: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP / B1), Lipoic acid, Coenzyme A (B5), FAD (B2), and NAD+ (B3) [mnemonic: TLCFN]. Elevated leucine is severely neurotoxic, causing cerebral edema and dystonia. Alloisoleucine is pathognomonic.

options.text: Biotin (derived from vitamin B7)
options.explanation: Biotin is the cofactor for carboxylases (pyruvate carboxylase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase), not BCKDH decarboxylation.

explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) complex. BCKDH metabolizes the alpha-keto acids derived from BRANCHED-CHAIN AMINO ACIDS: Leucine (alpha-ketoisocaproate), Isoleucine (alpha-keto-beta-methylvalerate), and Valine (alpha-ketoisovalerate). Like pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (alpha-KGDH), the BCKDH complex requires five obligatory cofactors: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP / B1), Lipoic acid, Coenzyme A (B5), FAD (B2), and NAD+ (B3) [mnemonic: TLCFN]. Elevated leucine is severely neurotoxic, causing cerebral edema and dystonia. Alloisoleucine is pathognomonic. Sweet maple syrup urine odor + dystonia/lethargy + high leucine/isoleucine/valine + alloisoleucine = MSUD -> BCKDH complex requires Thiamine pyrophosphate (B1).
objective: Understand and correctly identify the clinical, diagnostic, and pathophysiological principles of Maple Syrup Urine Disease BCKDH Complex Defect.

Sweet maple syrup urine odor + dystonia/lethargy + high leucine/isoleucine/valine + alloisoleucine = MSUD -> BCKDH complex requires Thiamine pyrophosphate (B1).

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Homocystinuria vs Marfan Syndrome Ectopia Lentis
stem: An 8-year-old tall, slender boy with cognitive impairment is evaluated for sudden painless loss of vision in his left eye. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy demonstrates downward and inward subluxation of the crystalline lens (inferonasal ectopia lentis). Physical examination reveals a marfanoid habitus, long thin fingers (arachnodactyly), high-arched palate, and pectus excavatum. Three days later, he develops acute right-sided hemiplegia; CT angiography of the head confirms an acute left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke. Laboratory evaluation shows: total plasma homocysteine 185 micromol/L (markedly elevated; normal < 15 micromol/L) and elevated serum methionine. Which of the following enzymes is deficient in this patient, and which vitamin cofactor trial is indicated?

options.text: Methionine synthase; requires a trial of ascorbic acid (vitamin C)
options.explanation: Methionine synthase deficiency elevates homocysteine but DEPRESSES methionine, whereas this patient has elevated methionine.

options.text: Methylene tetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR); requires a trial of cholecalciferol (vitamin D)
options.explanation: MTHFR deficiency impairs conversion of 5,10-methylene-THF to 5-methyl-THF; it elevates homocysteine but lowers methionine, and does not respond to vitamin D.

options.text: Fibrillin-1 microfibrillar protein; requires surgical aortic root replacement without vitamin therapy
options.explanation: Fibrillin-1 mutations cause autosomal dominant Marfan syndrome, which features superotemporal ('up and out') lens dislocation, normal cognition, normal homocysteine, and aortic root aneurysms.

options.text: Lysyl oxidase in the extracellular matrix; requires a trial of copper gluconate
options.explanation: Lysyl oxidase deficiency causes Menkes disease (kinky hair, hypotonia, low copper), not homocystinuria with downward lens subluxation and stroke.

options.text: Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS); requires a trial of pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
options.explanation: Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS), which condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine. Elevated homocysteine and methionine cause connective tissue disruption (fibrillin cross-linking interference) producing a marfanoid habitus. Crucial distinguishing features from Marfan syndrome include: (1) INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY (present in homocystinuria, absent in Marfan); (2) INFERONASAL ectopia lentis ('down and in' in homocystinuria vs 'up and out' superotemporal in Marfan); and (3) PREMATURE THROMBOEMBOLISM (deep vein thrombosis, stroke, myocardial infarction at young age due to endothelial toxicity). CBS requires PYRIDOXAL PHOSPHATE (vitamin B6) as a cofactor; ~50% of patients respond to high-dose vitamin B6 supplementation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 42-year-old man presents with chronic, progressive pain and stiffness in his lower back, hips, and knees. Physical examination reveals dark bluish-black pigmentation of the sclerae and ear cartilages (ochronosis). Spine radiographs demonstrate severe disc space narrowing with dense calcification of the intervertebral discs throughout the lumbar spine. His urine, upon standing on the laboratory benchtop for 4 hours, darkens from amber to a deep black color. Which of the following steps in amino acid metabolism is blocked in this patient?

options.text: Oxidation of homogentisic acid to maleylacetoacetic acid in the tyrosine degradation pathway
options.explanation: Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase. This enzyme degrades homogentisic acid (an intermediate in phenylalanine and tyrosine catabolism) into maleylacetoacetic acid. Excess homogentisic acid accumulates and is excreted in the urine, where it auto-oxidizes to benzoquinone acetic acid polymers, turning urine BLACK upon prolonged standing or exposure to alkaline air. Circulating homogentisic acid binds irreversibly to fibrillar collagen in connective tissues, causing bluish-black pigmentation (OCHRONOSIS) in ear cartilages and sclerae, and accelerating devastating degenerative OCHRONOTIC ARTHROPATHY with calcified intervertebral discs.

options.text: Decarboxylation of dopa to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase
options.explanation: Dopa decarboxylation produces catecholamines; defect does not cause black urine or ochronotic cartilage pigmentation.

options.text: Conversion of tyrosine to 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (dopa) by tyrosinase
options.explanation: Tyrosinase deficiency causes oculocutaneous albinism (lack of melanin pigment), the exact opposite of dark ochronotic pigmentation.

options.text: Transamination of phenylpyruvate to phenylalanine by phenylalanine aminotransferase
options.explanation: Phenylalanine aminotransferase transamination operates in reverse during PKU; it does not produce homogentisic acid or ochronosis.

options.text: Hydrolysis of fumarylacetoacetate into fumarate and acetoacetate in hepatocytes
options.explanation: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes tyrosinemia type 1 with acute hepatic failure and renal tubular dysfunction, not alkaptonuria.

explanation: Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase. This enzyme degrades homogentisic acid (an intermediate in phenylalanine and tyrosine catabolism) into maleylacetoacetic acid. Excess homogentisic acid accumulates and is excreted in the urine, where it auto-oxidizes to benzoquinone acetic acid polymers, turning urine BLACK upon prolonged standing or exposure to alkaline air. Urine turns black on standing + bluish-black ear/sclera pigment (ochronosis) + calcified intervertebral discs = Alkaptonuria -> homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency.

stem: A 3-day-old male newborn develops progressive somnolence, vomiting, tachypnea, and seizures. Laboratory evaluation reveals: arterial pH 7.52, PaCO2 22 mm Hg, bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (respiratory alkalosis), blood glucose 86 mg/dL (normal), and serum ammonia 850 micromol/L (severely elevated; normal < 50 micromol/L). Plasma amino acid analysis reveals markedly elevated glutamine and alanine, with undetectable citrulline. Urine organic acid analysis reveals a massive peak of orotic acid (420 mmol/mol creatinine; normal < 2). Which of the following is the mode of inheritance and underlying enzymatic defect in this infant?

options.text: Autosomal recessive; deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS-1) preventing initial ammonia incorporation
options.explanation: CPS-1 deficiency also causes severe hyperammonemia with low citrulline, but because carbamoyl phosphate cannot be synthesized, orotic acid is LOW or absent, distinguishing it from OTC.

options.text: X-linked recessive; deficiency of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) causing mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate accumulation that spills into cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis
options.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder and the ONLY ONE that is X-LINKED RECESSIVE (all others are autosomal recessive). In the mitochondrial matrix, OTC condenses carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline. When OTC is defective, excess mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate spills into the cytoplasm, where it enters the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway via cytoplasmic aspartate transcarbamoylase. This causes massive overproduction and urinary excretion of OROTIC ACID, accompanied by profound hyperammonemia (driving central hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis) and undetectable citrulline.

options.text: Autosomal recessive; deficiency of argininosuccinate synthetase causing massive citrullinemia
options.explanation: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency causes citrullinemia type 1 with MASSIVELY ELEVATED plasma citrulline, not undetectable citrulline.

options.text: Autosomal recessive; deficiency of uridine monophosphate (UMP) synthase causing orotic aciduria without hyperammonemia
options.explanation: UMP synthase deficiency causes hereditary orotic aciduria, which presents with megaloblastic anemia and normal serum ammonia, not lethal hyperammonemic encephalopathy.

options.text: Autosomal recessive; deficiency of arginase-1 causing isolated spastic diplegia without severe hyperammonemic crises
options.explanation: Arginase deficiency causes progressive spastic paraplegia and elevated arginine, with only mild, episodic hyperammonemia.

explanation: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder and the ONLY ONE that is X-LINKED RECESSIVE (all others are autosomal recessive). In the mitochondrial matrix, OTC condenses carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline. When OTC is defective, excess mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate spills into the cytoplasm, where it enters the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway via cytoplasmic aspartate transcarbamoylase. This causes massive overproduction and urinary excretion of OROTIC ACID, accompanied by profound hyperammonemia (driving central hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis) and undetectable citrulline. Neonatal hyperammonemia + respiratory alkalosis + undetectable citrulline + high urine orotic acid = OTC deficiency -> X-linked recessive, carbamoyl phosphate shunts to pyrimidines.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Hereditary Orotic Aciduria UMP Synthase Defect
stem: A 14-month-old girl is evaluated for severe pallor and failure to thrive. Physical examination demonstrates height and weight below the 3rd percentile and pale conjunctivae without hepatosplenomegaly or jaundice. Complete blood count demonstrates: hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL, MCV 112 fL (macrocytic), WBC count 4,800/microL, and platelet count 180,000/microL. Reticulocyte count is 0.4% (markedly depressed). Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels are within normal limits, and administration of high-dose intramuscular cobalamin and oral folic acid for 6 weeks produces no hematologic improvement. Urinalysis demonstrates needle-shaped crystals, and urine organic acid analysis reveals a massive excretion of orotic acid. Blood ammonia and blood glucose are completely normal. Which of the following dietary supplements will bypass the enzymatic block and cure the anemia in this child?

options.text: Oral citrulline and sodium phenylbutyrate
options.explanation: Citrulline and phenylbutyrate are used in urea cycle disorders to remove waste nitrogen, but do not supply pyrimidines for hereditary orotic aciduria.

options.text: Intramuscular pyridoxine (vitamin B6) and serine
options.explanation: Pyridoxine and serine are used in homocystinuria, not pyrimidine synthesis defects.

options.text: Oral uridine (or uridine triacetate)
options.explanation: Hereditary orotic aciduria is an autosomal recessive defect in UMP SYNTHASE (a bifunctional cytoplasmic enzyme possessing orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase activities). UMP synthase converts orotic acid to UMP in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. When UMP synthase is defective, pyrimidine starvation halts DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing erythroblasts, causing MEGALOBLASTIC ANEMIA refractory to B12 and folate. Excess orotic acid is excreted in urine, precipitating as crystals. Crucially, blood ammonia is NORMAL (distinguishing it from OTC deficiency). Electrocardiogram demonstrates strikingly high-voltage QRS complexes with a shortened PR interval across all limb and precordial leads. stem: A 2-year-old boy is evaluated for hepatomegaly and mild growth deceleration. His parents report that he becomes irritable if meals are delayed. options.text: Glycogen debranching enzyme (possessing amylo-alpha-1,6-glucosidase and 4-alpha-glucanotransferase activities)

stem: A 19-year-old collegiate sprinter presents with severe, painful muscle cramping in his calves and thighs during intense 100-meter sprints. If he rests briefly after initial cramping, he can continue running at a moderate pace with much less discomfort ('second-wind phenomenon'). Following his most recent race, his urine appeared dark red-brown; urinalysis reveals 3+ blood on dipstick with zero red blood cells on microscopic examination. Serum creatine kinase is 18,500 U/L. An ischemic forearm exercise test is performed: sequential blood samples from the exercising arm demonstrate a normal, brisk rise in venous ammonia levels, but the venous lactate concentration remains completely flat throughout exercise. Which of the following enzymes is deficient in this patient's myocytes?

options.text: Phosphofructokinase-1 in skeletal muscle (Tarui disease, GSD VII)
options.explanation: Tarui disease also causes exertional cramps and flat lactate curves, but impairs the second-wind phenomenon (blood glucose cannot enter glycolysis past PFK-1) and causes hemolytic anemia.

options.text: Myophosphorylase (skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase encoded by PYGM)
options.explanation: McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of myophosphorylase (skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase). Phosphorylase cleaves alpha-1,4-glycosidic bonds in glycogen to release glucose-1-phosphate for anaerobic glycolysis during intense exercise. Without myophosphorylase, muscle cells cannot mobilize glycogen, causing rapid ATP depletion, painful contractures, and rhabdomyolysis with dark myoglobinuria (dipstick positive for blood, zero RBCs). The 'second-wind phenomenon' occurs because after 10-15 minutes of exercise, increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and lipolysis deliver blood-borne glucose and free fatty acids to the working muscle, bypassing the blocked glycogenolysis. The ISCHEMIC FOREARM TEST demonstrates failure of venous lactate to rise (flat curve) while deamination of AMP to IMP produces a normal rise in ammonia.

options.text: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT II) in the mitochondrial inner membrane
options.explanation: CPT II deficiency impairs fatty acid oxidation during prolonged endurance exercise (marathons) or fasting, not brief anaerobic sprinting; forearm lactate curve is normal in CPT II.

options.text: Acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase in skeletal muscle lysosomes
options.explanation: Acid maltase deficiency causes Pompe disease (infantile cardiomyopathy or adult-onset limb-girdle weakness) without acute exercise-induced cramping or flat lactate curves.

options.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 alpha subunit in the mitochondrial matrix
options.explanation: PDH deficiency causes congenital lactic acidosis, microcephaly, and psychomotor delay, not exercise-induced myoglobinuria with a flat lactate curve.

stem: A 28-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish woman presents with progressive fatigue, left upper quadrant abdominal discomfort, and easy bruisability. Radiographs of the distal femurs demonstrate cortical thinning with widening of the metaphyses resembling an 'Erlenmeyer flask' deformity. Bone marrow aspiration reveals numerous enlarged, lipid-laden macrophages with an abundant fibrillary cytoplasm resembling 'wrinkled tissue paper' or 'crinkled silk'. options.explanation: Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease, characterized by foamy macrophages (not crinkled paper), hepatosplenomegaly, and a cherry-red macular spot.

options.text: Deficiency of hexosaminidase A; accumulation of GM2 ganglioside
options.explanation: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, presenting with neurodegeneration and cherry-red macula, WITHOUT hepatosplenomegaly or bone deformities.

options.text: Deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase); accumulation of glucocerebroside
options.explanation: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disease (autosomal recessive, highly prevalent in Ashkenazi Jewish populations), caused by mutations in the GBA gene encoding beta-glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase). options.explanation: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease (X-linked), presenting with angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, and renal failure, without Erlenmeyer flask deformities.

options.text: Deficiency of galactocerebrosidase; accumulation of galactocerebroside and psychosine

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with severe, burning pain in his palms and soles (acroparesthesias) triggered by exercise and warm weather. He reports an inability to sweat normally (hypohidrosis). Physical examination reveals clusters of non-blanching, dark red-to-purple punctate macules and papules in a 'bathing trunk' distribution across the groin, umbilicus, and lower abdomen (angiokeratomas). Slit-lamp examination demonstrates whorl-like corneal opacities (cornea verticillata). Urinalysis shows 2+ proteinuria; polarized light microscopy of the urine sediment demonstrates birefringent oval fat bodies with a 'Maltese cross' pattern. If left untreated, which of the following end-organ complications represents the most common cause of premature mortality in this disorder?

options.text: Fulminant hepatic failure secondary to intrahepatic canalicular phospholipid precipitation
options.explanation: Fabry disease spares hepatic synthetic function; liver failure is not a feature of globotriaosylceramide accumulation.

options.text: Severe restrictive lung disease resulting from diffuse alveolar septal glucosylceramide fibrosis
options.explanation: Pulmonary fibrosis is not the characteristic pathology; Fabry disease primarily causes renal, cardiovascular, and cerebrovascular disease.

options.text: Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome) due to microvascular calcification
options.explanation: Adrenal hemorrhage is caused by meningococcemia or severe sepsis, not metabolic glycosphingolipid storage.

options.text: Spontaneous splenic rupture driven by massive subcapsular reticuloendothelial histiocytosis
options.explanation: Splenomegaly is absent or minimal in Fabry disease; life-threatening complications are renal and cardiac.

Early manifestations in adolescence include episodic neuropathic pain (acroparesthesias), hypohidrosis, angiokeratomas, and cornea verticillata. With age, Gb3 vascular occlusions cause progressive glomerulosclerosis (proteinuria progressing to ESRD in the 30s-40s), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, and early ischemic strokes, which represent the major causes of premature mortality.

stem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive in her crib. She developed a mild viral gastroenteritis yesterday with poor oral intake. Physical examination shows an unconscious toddler with hepatomegaly and hyporeflexia. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: blood glucose 24 mg/dL (severe hypoglycemia), serum bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, and normal serum lactate. Urinalysis demonstrates zero ketones (absence of acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate). Plasma acylcarnitine profiling reveals markedly elevated octanoylcarnitine (C8), with significant elevations in hexanoylcarnitine (C6) and decanoylcarnitine (C10). Urine organic acid analysis reveals prominent dicarboxylic acids (adipic, suberic, and sebacic acids). Which of the following is the underlying biochemical defect in this child?

options.text: Impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids (C6 to C12) due to medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
options.explanation: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is the most common inborn error of fatty acid oxidation (autosomal recessive). MCAD catalyzes the first step of mitochondrial beta-oxidation for medium-chain fatty acids (6 to 12 carbons). During periods of fasting, glycogen stores deplete and the body must rely on fatty acid beta-oxidation to generate acetyl-CoA for ketone body synthesis and ATP to power gluconeogenesis. When MCAD is deficient, beta-oxidation stalls: (1) Acetyl-CoA is not generated -> failure of ketogenesis -> HYPOKETOTIC HYPOGLYCEMIA; (2) Unmetabolized fatty acids accumulate as C8-C10 acylcarnitines; and (3) Excess medium-chain fatty acids undergo omega-oxidation in peroxisomes, producing urinary DICARBOXYLIC ACIDS. Treatment requires avoiding prolonged fasting and high-carbohydrate meals.

options.text: Deficiency of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) in the outer mitochondrial membrane
options.explanation: CPT-I deficiency impairs long-chain fatty acid entry into mitochondria, elevating free carnitine with low acylcarnitines, unlike the elevated C8-acylcarnitines of MCAD.

options.text: Deficiency of hormone-sensitive lipase in white adipocytes preventing lipolysis
options.explanation: Hormone-sensitive lipase deficiency impairs peripheral free fatty acid release; serum acylcarnitines and dicarboxylic acids would not be elevated.

options.text: Deficiency of mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase in hepatocytes preventing ketone synthesis with normal beta-oxidation
options.explanation: HMG-CoA synthase deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia, but beta-oxidation is intact, so acylcarnitines (C8) and dicarboxylic acids are normal.

options.text: Deficiency of peroxisomal phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase impairing alpha-oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids
options.explanation: Phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency causes Refsum disease (accumulation of phytanic acid causing retinitis pigmentosa and ataxia), not hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

explanation: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is the most common inborn error of fatty acid oxidation (autosomal recessive). MCAD catalyzes the first step of mitochondrial beta-oxidation for medium-chain fatty acids (6 to 12 carbons). During periods of fasting, glycogen stores deplete and the body must rely on fatty acid beta-oxidation to generate acetyl-CoA for ketone body synthesis and ATP to power gluconeogenesis. When MCAD is deficient, beta-oxidation stalls: (1) Acetyl-CoA is not generated -> failure of ketogenesis -> HYPOKETOTIC HYPOGLYCEMIA; (2) Unmetabolized fatty acids accumulate as C8-C10 acylcarnitines; and (3) Excess medium-chain fatty acids undergo omega-oxidation in peroxisomes, producing urinary DICARBOXYLIC ACIDS. Treatment requires avoiding prolonged fasting and high-carbohydrate meals. Fasting hypoglycemia + ABSENCE of ketones + elevated C8-octanoylcarnitine + urinary dicarboxylic acids = MCAD deficiency -> impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation.

Fasting hypoglycemia + ABSENCE of ketones + elevated C8-octanoylcarnitine + urinary dicarboxylic acids = MCAD deficiency -> impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Systemic Primary Carnitine Deficiency OCTN2 Defect
stem: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive muscle weakness, lethargy, and recurrent episodes of fasting hypoglycemia. Physical examination reveals poor muscle tone and hepatomegaly. Echocardiography demonstrates dilated cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. Laboratory studies reveal: blood glucose 32 mg/dL, absence of urinary ketones, serum free carnitine 2.4 micromol/L (severely depressed; normal 25-54 micromol/L), and total carnitine 3.8 micromol/L. Urine organic acid analysis shows no dicarboxylic acids. Serum acylcarnitine profile is globally depressed across all chain lengths. Genetic analysis demonstrates a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the SLC22A5 gene encoding the OCTN2 high-affinity sodium-dependent carnitine transporter. Which of the following describes the cellular consequence of this transporter defect?

options.text: Inability of the malate-aspartate shuttle to transfer reducing equivalents into the mitochondrial matrix
options.explanation: The malate-aspartate shuttle transfers NADH across the mitochondrial membrane for oxidative phosphorylation, and does not involve carnitine.

options.text: Failure of renal tubular carnitine reabsorption and cellular carnitine uptake prevents the carnitine shuttle from transporting long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation
options.explanation: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in SLC22A5 encoding the OCTN2 organic cation/carnitine transporter. OCTN2 mediates high-affinity sodium-dependent carnitine uptake across the plasma membrane of enterocytes, myocytes, hepatocytes, and renal proximal tubular cells. Without OCTN2, renal tubular reabsorption of carnitine drops from >98% to <10%, causing urinary carnitine wasting and profound systemic carnitine depletion. Without intracellular carnitine, the CARNITINE SHUTTLE (CPT-I / CACT / CPT-II) cannot transport activated long-chain acyl-CoA into the mitochondrial matrix. This halts beta-oxidation, depriving cardiac and skeletal muscle of their primary fuel and producing dilated cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Lifelong high-dose oral L-carnitine is curative.

options.text: Failure of the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle to reoxidize cytosolic NADH in skeletal muscle
options.explanation: The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle uses FAD to transfer electrons to CoQ, independent of carnitine.

options.text: Defective citrate lyase activity preventing export of acetyl-CoA for cytoplasmic fatty acid synthesis
options.explanation: Citrate lyase operates in fatty acid synthesis (anabolism), not beta-oxidation fatty acid transport.

options.text: Inactivation of hormone-sensitive lipase preventing release of unesterified fatty acids from adipocytes
options.explanation: Hormone-sensitive lipase releases fatty acids into blood; carnitine deficiency impairs intracellular uptake and mitochondrial transport.

explanation: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in SLC22A5 encoding the OCTN2 organic cation/carnitine transporter. OCTN2 mediates high-affinity sodium-dependent carnitine uptake across the plasma membrane of enterocytes, myocytes, hepatocytes, and renal proximal tubular cells. Without OCTN2, renal tubular reabsorption of carnitine drops from >98% to <10%, causing urinary carnitine wasting and profound systemic carnitine depletion. Without intracellular carnitine, the CARNITINE SHUTTLE (CPT-I / CACT / CPT-II) cannot transport activated long-chain acyl-CoA into the mitochondrial matrix. This halts beta-oxidation, depriving cardiac and skeletal muscle of their primary fuel and producing dilated cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Lifelong high-dose oral L-carnitine is curative. Dilated cardiomyopathy + hypoketotic hypoglycemia + severely low plasma/tissue carnitine + OCTN2 mutation = Systemic primary carnitine deficiency.
objective: Understand and correctly identify the clinical, diagnostic, and pathophysiological principles of Systemic Primary Carnitine Deficiency OCTN2 Defect.
keyPoints: Systemic Primary Carnitine Deficiency OCTN2 Defect
Dilated cardiomyopathy + hypoketotic hypoglycemia + severely low plasma/tissue carnitine + OCTN2 mutation = Systemic primary carnitine deficiency.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 10-month-old infant is evaluated for chronic foul-smelling, bulky, greasy diarrhea, severe abdominal distention, and failure to thrive. Physical examination reveals a wasted infant with dry skin, mild ataxia, and absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities. Laboratory studies show: total serum cholesterol 28 mg/dL (markedly depressed; normal 120-200 mg/dL), serum triglycerides 14 mg/dL (markedly depressed; normal 40-150 mg/dL), and undetectable serum apolipoprotein B. Peripheral blood smear reveals numerous erythrocytes with irregular, thorny projections of variable length and width distributed unevenly over the cell surface (acanthocytes / spur cells). Duodenal biopsy shows enterocytes with normal villus architecture but packed with clear cytoplasmic lipid vacuoles that stain strongly with Oil Red O. Which of the following is the underlying molecular defect in this infant?

options.text: Autosomal dominant mutation in the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor gene causing impaired hepatic endocytosis
options.explanation: LDL receptor mutations cause familial hypercholesterolemia (elevated LDL and premature CAD), the exact opposite of abetalipoproteinemia.

options.text: Complete absence of apolipoprotein C-II preventing lipoprotein lipase activation
options.explanation: ApoC-II deficiency causes familial hyperchylomicronemia (Type I dyslipidemia) with massive hypertriglyceridemia, eruptive xanthomas, and pancreatitis, not undetectable lipids.

options.text: Homozygous inactivating mutation in the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP) gene preventing the assembly and secretion of apoB-containing chylomicrons and VLDL
options.explanation: Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the MTTP gene encoding the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein. MTTP is an essential chaperone in the ER lumen that transfers triglycerides, phospholipids, and cholesteryl esters onto newly synthesized APOLIPOPROTEIN B (apoB-48 in enterocytes and apoB-100 in hepatocytes). In the absence of MTTP, enterocytes cannot assemble or excrete CHYLOMICRONS, and hepatocytes cannot secrete VLDL. Dietary lipids become trapped within mucosal enterocytes, appearing as lipid-laden enterocytes on biopsy. Severe malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) ensues. Lack of vitamin E causes spinocerebellar ataxia, while membrane lipid imbalance produces ACANTHOCYTOSIS.

options.text: Inactivating mutation in the hepatic lipase gene preventing intermediate-density lipoprotein conversion
options.explanation: Hepatic lipase deficiency causes Type III dyslipidemia with elevated IDL/chylomicron remnants, not fat malabsorption with acanthocytes.

options.text: Deficiency of lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) preventing high-density lipoprotein maturation
options.explanation: LCAT deficiency causes 'fish-eye' disease (corneal opacities, hemolytic anemia, renal failure) with normal chylomicron assembly.

explanation: Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the MTTP gene encoding the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein. MTTP is an essential chaperone in the ER lumen that transfers triglycerides, phospholipids, and cholesteryl esters onto newly synthesized APOLIPOPROTEIN B (apoB-48 in enterocytes and apoB-100 in hepatocytes). In the absence of MTTP, enterocytes cannot assemble or excrete CHYLOMICRONS, and hepatocytes cannot secrete VLDL. Dietary lipids become trapped within mucosal enterocytes, appearing as lipid-laden enterocytes on biopsy. Severe malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) ensues. Lack of vitamin E causes spinocerebellar ataxia, while membrane lipid imbalance produces ACANTHOCYTOSIS. Greasy diarrhea + near-zero cholesterol/triglycerides + zero apoB + lipid-laden enterocytes + acanthocytes = Abetalipoproteinemia -> MTTP mutation.

Greasy diarrhea + near-zero cholesterol/triglycerides + zero apoB + lipid-laden enterocytes + acanthocytes = Abetalipoproteinemia -> MTTP mutation.

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Vitamin B12 vs Folate Methylmalonic Acid Biomarker
stem: A 64-year-old strict vegan woman presents with progressive numbness and tingling in her feet, unsteady gait, and memory difficulties. Physical examination reveals pale conjunctivae, loss of vibration sense and proprioception in both lower extremities, spasticity, and bilateral extensor plantar responses (positive Babinski sign). Complete blood count demonstrates: hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, MCV 114 fL (macrocytic), WBC count 3,200/microL, and platelet count 110,000/microL. Peripheral blood smear confirms hypersegmented neutrophils (>=6 lobes). Serum folate concentration is normal. Which of the following biochemical profiles of plasma methylmalonic acid (MMA) and total homocysteine definitively confirms the diagnosis of cobalamin deficiency over folate deficiency?

options.text: Normal methylmalonic acid and markedly elevated homocysteine
options.explanation: Normal MMA with elevated homocysteine is the exact metabolic signature of FOLATE DEFICIENCY, which does not impair methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

options.text: Markedly elevated methylmalonic acid and completely normal homocysteine
options.explanation: Elevated MMA with normal homocysteine is not seen in dietary B12 deficiency because cobalamin is required for both enzymes.

options.text: Markedly depressed methylmalonic acid and markedly depressed homocysteine
options.explanation: Both metabolites accumulate when their catabolic enzymes lack cofactors; they are never depressed in deficiency states.

options.text: Markedly elevated methylmalonic acid and markedly elevated homocysteine
options.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) serves as an essential cofactor for exactly two human enzymes: (1) METHIONINE SYNTHASE (cytosol), which transfers a methyl group from 5-methyl-THF to homocysteine, generating methionine and regenerating free THF; and (2) METHYLMALONYL-CoA MUTASE (mitochondria), which isomerizes methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. In cobalamin deficiency, both pathways fail, leading to ELEVATED HOMOCYSTEINE and ELEVATED METHYLMALONIC ACID (MMA). In contrast, FOLATE DEFICIENCY only affects the methionine synthase step; therefore, folate deficiency produces ELEVATED HOMOCYSTEINE BUT NORMAL MMA. Furthermore, only cobalamin deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (due to impaired myelin maintenance from accumulated methylmalonic acid and abnormal fatty acids).

options.text: Normal methylmalonic acid and normal homocysteine
options.explanation: Normal levels of both metabolites rule out active cellular deficiency of both vitamin B12 and folate.

In cobalamin deficiency, both pathways fail, leading to ELEVATED HOMOCYSTEINE and ELEVATED METHYLMALONIC ACID (MMA). In contrast, FOLATE DEFICIENCY only affects the methionine synthase step; therefore, folate deficiency produces ELEVATED HOMOCYSTEINE BUT NORMAL MMA. Macrocytic anemia + hypersegmented neutrophils + subacute combined degeneration = B12 deficiency -> BOTH methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are elevated.

stem: A 54-year-old chronic alcoholic man is brought to the emergency department after being found disoriented on the street. Physical examination shows an emaciated man with horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus palsy (abducens nerve impairment), and marked gait ataxia. He is oriented only to his name and confabulates when asked about recent events. Before administering intravenous dextrose, the physician orders intravenous thiamine. Which of the following erythrocyte enzyme assays would demonstrate a >25% increase in enzymatic activity upon in vitro addition of thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), definitively confirming this patient's underlying deficiency?

options.text: Erythrocyte glutathione reductase in the pentose phosphate antioxidant pathway
options.explanation: Glutathione reductase requires flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD, derived from vitamin B2 / riboflavin); an increase in activity upon adding FAD measures riboflavin deficiency.

options.text: Erythrocyte aspartate aminotransferase in transamination metabolism
options.explanation: Aspartate aminotransferase requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP / vitamin B6); the activation assay with PLP measures vitamin B6 deficiency.

options.text: Erythrocyte glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in NADPH generation
options.explanation: G6PD activity requires NADP+; it is an intrinsic genetic enzyme deficiency, not a vitamin-dependent functional cofactor assay.

options.text: Erythrocyte pyruvate kinase in the terminal step of glycolysis
options.explanation: Pyruvate kinase requires ADP and K+/Mg2+; it does not utilize thiamine pyrophosphate.

options.text: Erythrocyte transketolase in the non-oxidative branch of the hexose monophosphate shunt
options.explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is phosphorylated to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), an essential cofactor for: (1) PYRUVATE DEHYDROGENASE (linking glycolysis to the TCA cycle); (2) ALPHA-KETOGLUTARATE DEHYDROGENASE (TCA cycle); (3) BRANCHED-CHAIN ALPHA-KETO ACID DEHYDROGENASE (BCAA breakdown); and (4) TRANSKETOLASE (hexose monophosphate shunt). In chronic alcoholism, impaired intestinal absorption and storage deplete thiamine, precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy (triad of encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, and gait ataxia) and Korsakoff psychosis (confabulation, anterograde amnesia). Giving glucose without thiamine worsens neurotoxicity because glucose oxidation consumes residual TPP. The functional test confirming thiamine deficiency is the ERYTHROCYTE TRANSKETOLASE ACTIVATION ASSAY: patient hemolysate is incubated with TPP; an increase in transketolase activity >25% (TPP effect) confirms severe thiamine deficiency.

In chronic alcoholism, impaired intestinal absorption and storage deplete thiamine, precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy (triad of encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, and gait ataxia) and Korsakoff psychosis (confabulation, anterograde amnesia). Giving glucose without thiamine worsens neurotoxicity because glucose oxidation consumes residual TPP. The functional test confirming thiamine deficiency is the ERYTHROCYTE TRANSKETOLASE ACTIVATION ASSAY: patient hemolysate is incubated with TPP; an increase in transketolase activity >25% (TPP effect) confirms severe thiamine deficiency. Chronic alcoholic + ataxia/nystagmus/confusion = Wernicke encephalopathy -> thiamine deficiency confirmed by erythrocyte transketolase activation with TPP.

Chronic alcoholic + ataxia/nystagmus/confusion = Wernicke encephalopathy -> thiamine deficiency confirmed by erythrocyte transketolase activation with TPP.

topic: Niacin Deficiency Pellagra and Hartnup Disease
stem: A 36-year-old homeless man presents with a painful, symmetric, hyperpigmented, scaly rash on the sun-exposed areas of his neck and upper chest ('Casal necklace'), as well as the dorsum of both hands. He also reports persistent watery diarrhea for 3 weeks. During the interview, he exhibits memory loss, disorientation, and paranoia. Further testing demonstrates normal dietary intake of essential amino acids except for severe malnutrition. Which of the following amino acid precursors can normally be converted endogenously into the deficient vitamin, and what two vitamin-derived cofactors are strictly required for this conversion?

options.text: Tryptophan; requires riboflavin (FAD, vitamin B2) and pyridoxine (PLP, vitamin B6) to synthesize nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)
options.explanation: Pellagra is caused by deficiency of NIACIN (vitamin B3), leading to the classic '4 Ds': Dermatitis (photosensitive Casal necklace, hyperkeratosis on hands/feet), Diarrhea, Dementia (encephalopathy, paranoia), and Death. Niacin forms NAD+ and NADP+, critical cofactors for cellular dehydrogenases and ADP-ribosylation. Humans can synthesize niacin endogenously from the essential amino acid TRYPTOPHAN (~60 mg tryptophan yields 1 mg niacin). This complex multi-step hepatic pathway requires two critical vitamin cofactors: RIBOFLAVIN (FAD, vitamin B2) for kynurenine 3-monooxygenase, and PYRIDOXINE (PLP, vitamin B6) for kynureninase. Deficiency of B2, B6, or tryptophan (as in Hartnup disease or carcinoid syndrome where tryptophan is shunted to serotonin) can precipitate secondary pellagra.

options.text: Phenylalanine; requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) and iron (Fe2+) to synthesize nicotinic acid
options.explanation: Phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine by phenylalanine hydroxylase; it does not yield niacin.

options.text: Methionine; requires adenosylcobalamin (vitamin B12) and folate to synthesize niacinamide
options.explanation: Methionine participates in methylation reactions and homocysteine metabolism; it does not synthesize niacin.

options.text: Histidine; requires tetrahydrofolate (THF) and ascorbic acid to synthesize nicotinamide
options.explanation: Histidine is degraded to glutamate via formiminoglutamate (FIGLU); it is not a precursor for niacin.

options.text: Tyrosine; requires copper and vitamin C to synthesize nicotinic acid mononucleotide
options.explanation: Tyrosine is converted into catecholamines and melanin; it does not enter the kynurenine pathway to form niacin.

explanation: Pellagra is caused by deficiency of NIACIN (vitamin B3), leading to the classic '4 Ds': Dermatitis (photosensitive Casal necklace, hyperkeratosis on hands/feet), Diarrhea, Dementia (encephalopathy, paranoia), and Death. Niacin forms NAD+ and NADP+, critical cofactors for cellular dehydrogenases and ADP-ribosylation. Humans can synthesize niacin endogenously from the essential amino acid TRYPTOPHAN (~60 mg tryptophan yields 1 mg niacin). This complex multi-step hepatic pathway requires two critical vitamin cofactors: RIBOFLAVIN (FAD, vitamin B2) for kynurenine 3-monooxygenase, and PYRIDOXINE (PLP, vitamin B6) for kynureninase. Deficiency of B2, B6, or tryptophan (as in Hartnup disease or carcinoid syndrome where tryptophan is shunted to serotonin) can precipitate secondary pellagra. Casal necklace rash + watery diarrhea + dementia = Pellagra (Niacin / B3 deficiency) -> synthesized from Tryptophan requiring B2 (riboflavin) and B6 (pyridoxine).

subject: Biochemistry
topic: Scurvy and Prolyl Hydroxylase Collagen Defect
stem: A 72-year-old widower who lives alone on a diet consisting exclusively of canned tea and white toast presents with severe lethargy, easy bruisability, and lower extremity pain. Physical examination shows swollen, purple, spongy gingiva that bleeds with minor touch, multiple perifollicular hemorrhages with corkscrew hairs on both lower extremities, and large ecchymoses over the calves. Radiographs show subperiosteal hemorrhages along the tibias. A deficiency of which of the following substances causes this condition, and what is its specific molecular function inside the rough endoplasmic reticulum?

options.text: Copper; acts as a prosthetic group for extracellular lysyl oxidase to form covalent aldol cross-links between tropocollagen molecules
options.explanation: Copper is the cofactor for extracellular lysyl oxidase (defective in Menkes disease), not prolyl hydroxylase inside the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

options.text: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C); maintains the Fe2+ iron cofactor of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in the reduced state, enabling cross-linking of procollagen alpha-chains into a stable triple helix
options.explanation: Scurvy is caused by deficiency of ASCORBIC ACID (vitamin C). Inside the rough endoplasmic reticulum, newly synthesized pro-alpha collagen chains undergo post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, catalyzed by PROLYL HYDROXYLASE and LYSYL HYDROXYLASE. These enzymes require ferrous iron (Fe2+) and alpha-ketoglutarate. Ascorbic acid acts as a specific reducing agent to reduce oxidized Fe3+ back to catalytic Fe2+. Hydroxyproline residues are essential for forming interchain hydrogen bonds that stabilize the COLLAGEN TRIPLE HELIX. Without vitamin C, defective procollagen cannot form a stable triple helix and undergoes intracellular degradation. Blood vessels become fragile, producing gingival bleeding, perifollicular corkscrew hemorrhages, and subperiosteal hematomas.

options.text: Zinc; acts as a cofactor for matrix metalloproteinases cleaving non-helical terminal propeptides
options.explanation: Zinc is required for MMPs and procollagen peptidases, but scurvy is caused by ascorbic acid deficiency affecting prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation.

options.text: Vitamin K; enables gamma-carboxylation of glutamic acid residues on vascular basement membrane laminin
options.explanation: Vitamin K mediates gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X, C, S), not collagen hydroxylation.

options.text: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6); catalyzes the condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA during collagen strand synthesis
options.explanation: Pyridoxine is the cofactor for ALAS in heme synthesis, not collagen synthesis.

explanation: Scurvy is caused by deficiency of ASCORBIC ACID (vitamin C). Inside the rough endoplasmic reticulum, newly synthesized pro-alpha collagen chains undergo post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, catalyzed by PROLYL HYDROXYLASE and LYSYL HYDROXYLASE. These enzymes require ferrous iron (Fe2+) and alpha-ketoglutarate. Ascorbic acid acts as a specific reducing agent to reduce oxidized Fe3+ back to catalytic Fe2+. Hydroxyproline residues are essential for forming interchain hydrogen bonds that stabilize the COLLAGEN TRIPLE HELIX. Without vitamin C, defective procollagen cannot form a stable triple helix and undergoes intracellular degradation. Blood vessels become fragile, producing gingival bleeding, perifollicular corkscrew hemorrhages, and subperiosteal hematomas. Bleeding gums + corkscrew hairs + perifollicular hemorrhages = Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency) -> keeps Fe2+ reduced for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylases in RER.

Bleeding gums + corkscrew hairs + perifollicular hemorrhages = Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency) -> keeps Fe2+ reduced for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylases in RER.

topic: Vitamin D Toxicity in Granulomatous Disease 1-Alpha-Hydroxylase
stem: A 44-year-old woman with pulmonary sarcoidosis presents with severe constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, and confusion after spending 2 weeks on a sunny beach vacation. Physical examination reveals clear lungs, dry mucous membranes, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest radiograph. Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum calcium 13.6 mg/dL (severe hypercalcemia; normal 8.5-10.2 mg/dL), serum phosphate 4.8 mg/dL (elevated; normal 2.5-4.5 mg/dL), serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) < 4 pg/mL (suppressed; normal 10-65 pg/mL), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 38 ng/mL (normal 30-80 ng/mL), and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D 145 pg/mL (markedly elevated; normal 20-60 pg/mL). Which of the following is the cellular mechanism responsible for the elevation of the active vitamin D metabolite in this patient?

options.explanation: PTHrP secretion causes humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (squamous cell lung cancer); in sarcoidosis, hypercalcemia is mediated by 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and PTHrP is undetectable.

stem: A 23-year-old woman taking high-dose oral isotretinoin for severe cystic acne presents with daily pulsatile headaches, nausea, and transient visual obscurations (vision blacking out for a few seconds when bending over). Physical examination shows an acne-free face with prominent cheilitis (dry lips) and clear lung fields. Neurological examination reveals bilateral abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy and bilateral papilledema with blurring of the optic disc margins. Brain MRI and MR venography are completely normal, showing no mass, hydrocephalus, or dural venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture demonstrates an opening pressure of 340 mm H2O (markedly elevated; normal < 200 mm H2O) with normal CSF cell counts, glucose, and protein. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of action of the medication causing this condition, and what is its most devastating teratogenic effect if taken during early pregnancy?

options.text: Selective blockade of the sodium-iodide symporter; causes congenital hypothyroidism and severe dwarfism
options.explanation: Sodium-iodide symporter blockade is caused by perchlorate/thiocyanate, not retinoids.

options.text: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase halting thymidylate synthesis; causes neural tube closure failure (spina bifida)
options.explanation: Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate, not vitamin A derivatives.

options.text: Alkylating DNA cross-linking in rapidly dividing cells; causes limb reduction phocomelia and amelia
options.explanation: Phocomelia is the classic teratogenic defect of thalidomide, not isotretinoin.

options.text: Binding to nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RAR) and retinoid X receptors (RXR) to regulate gene transcription; causes pseudotumor cerebri and neural crest cell migration defects leading to craniofacial dysmorphism, thymic aplasia, and conotruncal cardiac anomalies
options.explanation: Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) is a synthetic vitamin A derivative that binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RAR) and retinoid X receptors (RXR) acting as ligand-activated transcription factors. Vitamin A toxicity and retinoids characteristically cause PSEUDOTUMOR CEREBRI (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) with papilledema, elevated ICP (>250 mm H2O), and CN VI palsy. Retinoids are severely TERATOGENIC: during embryogenesis, retinoic acid gradients govern NEURAL CREST CELL migration. Isotretinoin embryopathy includes microtia/anotia (external ear absence), cleft palate, thymic aplasia, and conotruncal heart defects (transposition of great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot). Two negative pregnancy tests and strict contraception (iPLEDGE) are mandatory.

options.text: Competitive antagonism of the endothelin-A receptor; causes severe renal tubular dysgenesis and oligohydramnios
options.explanation: Renal tubular dysgenesis with oligohydramnios (Potter sequence) is caused by ACE inhibitors and ARBs, not retinoids.

stem: An 82-year-old hospitalized woman who has been receiving total parenteral nutrition without vitamin additives and broad-spectrum intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for 16 days develops bleeding from her central line site and hematuria. She has no prior personal or family bleeding history. Coagulation profile reveals: PT 26 seconds (INR 2.8; normal 0.9-1.1), aPTT 44 seconds (mildly prolonged; normal 25-35 seconds), and platelet count 240,000/microL. A 1:1 mixing study demonstrates immediate normalization of both the PT and aPTT. Subcutaneous administration of phytonadione completely corrects the PT and aPTT within 18 hours. Which of the following post-translational modifications was defective in this patient's hepatocytes, and which clotting factor's short half-life explains the earlier and more profound prolongation of the PT compared to the aPTT?

options.text: Beta-hydroxylation of aspartic acid residues in epidermal growth factor-like domains; factor X has the shortest half-life (~40 hours)
options.explanation: Beta-hydroxylation does not depend on vitamin K; factor VII has the shortest half-life, not factor X.

options.text: O-linked glycosylation of serine and threonine residues in the catalytic domain; factor IX has the shortest half-life (~24 hours)
options.explanation: Vitamin K mediates gamma-carboxylation of glutamic acid, not glycosylation.

options.text: Sulfation of tyrosine residues by trans-Golgi sulfotransferases; factor II (prothrombin) has the shortest half-life (~60 hours)
options.explanation: Prothrombin has the LONGEST half-life (~60 hours) among the vitamin K factors; factor VII is shortest.

options.text: Proteolytic cleavage of carboxy-terminal propeptides in the endoplasmic reticulum; factor VIII has the shortest half-life
options.explanation: Factor VIII is not vitamin K-dependent and is stabilized by vWF.

options.text: Gamma-glutamyl carboxylation of amino-terminal glutamic acid residues to form calcium-binding Gla domains on clotting factors; factor VII has the shortest half-life (~4 to 6 hours)
options.explanation: Vitamin K is an essential cofactor for hepatic GAMMA-GLUTAMYL CARBOXYLASE. This enzyme converts glutamic acid (Glu) residues into gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) residues on coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as protein C and protein S. The negative Gla domains are required to bind Ca2+, which anchors these factors to negatively charged platelet phospholipids. Vitamin K deficiency occurs in hospitalized patients on antibiotics (loss of gut flora) and poor diet/TPN. The PROTHROMBIN TIME (PT) prolongs earlier and more dramatically than the aPTT because FACTOR VII HAS THE SHORTEST HALF-LIFE (~4-6 hours) of all coagulation factors, depleting rapidly before factors II, IX, or X.
